title: Orchestrator: tool result staging, injection model, and recursion mitigation
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Existing tool execution loop allows uncontrolled result injection and recursive tool invocation patterns that can cause live request amplification, infinite loops, or inconsistent structured outputs when used with streaming responses and older SDK compatibility layers. This ticket scopes a runtime-level staging and injection model to make single-request multi-tool flows deterministic, observable, and safe while preserving streaming and function-calling UX.

Goals: (1) Introduce a 'staging buffer' for tool outputs that separates tool execution from final response assembly so we can validate and sanitize injections before committing to the response stream. (2) Implement loop/recursion detection with configurable limits and graceful fallback policies. (3) Ensure compatibility with SDKs that expect immediate synchronous tool returns by providing a backward-compatible adapter. (4) Add observability and metrics to detect recurring loop patterns and operator-reachable debugging artifacts.

Out of scope: full rewrite of tool SDKs, persistent storage of intermediate tool state beyond request lifespan, and changes to customer-facing API surface for structured outputs (that will be handled in a follow-up).
technical_design:
Overview: The orchestrator will run a two-phase tool execution loop per request: (A) speculative execution phase where tools may be invoked and their raw outputs written to a per-request staging area (in-memory KV with strict size limits), and (B) injection commit phase where the orchestrator validates structured contracts, runs sanitization, enforces idempotency, and then applies a committed snapshot to the streaming output.

Staging mechanics: Each tool call writes a staging record: {tool_id, invocation_id, worker_node, raw_result_blob, schema_hint, timestamp, parent_invocation}. Staging is append-only for the request lifespan and garbage-collected at end of request. Records are signed with an HMAC using a per-request nonce to detect tampering if reprocessed.

Injection model: Executors propose an 'injection bundle' describing where in the response the tool result should be applied (prefix, suffix, structured-field path) and a contract pointer (structured output schema version). The orchestrator validates the bundle against the current route's allowed injection policies and the schema pointer. If valid, the commit phase applies the bundle atomically to the assembled response and emits a stream delta to the client. For streaming, deltas are queued and rate-limited to respect latency SLOs.

Loop/recursion guards: 1) Invocation depth cap (configurable per-route, default 6). 2) Visited-signature set: a bounded Bloom filter of (tool_id, normalized_input_hash) per request to detect re-invocations with identical inputs. 3) Wall-clock time cap and token budget cap for tool-driven subflows. 4) On detection, orchestrator rejects the new invocation with a structured error code, annotates the staging log, and triggers fallback policies (no-op, use cached result, or escalate to human-review queue for long-running requests).

Compatibility adapter: For SDK versions that expect synchronous tool returns (legacy clients), the orchestrator provides a compatibility path that waits for commit-phase acceptance for a short bounded window (default 800ms). If commit doesn't complete in window, legacy adapter returns a 'deferred-commit' response that contains a stable reference (commit_id) and a follow-up streaming URL or polling token. This preserves semantics while preventing blocking the orchestrator for unbounded time.

Sanitization & structured outputs: The commit-phase runs schema validation and a sanitization pipeline (trim, canonicalize types, redact secrets based on disclosure policy). If validation fails, a structured validation_error is returned describing the failing field and fallback applied.

Observability: Emit metrics: tool_invocations, staged_records_count, commit_latency_p50/p95, loop_detections, loop_break_actions, compatibility_adapter_timeouts. Persist per-request staging snapshot to ephemeral logs for 30s post-request to aid debugging when loop detection fires.

Operational toggles: feature flags to disable staging for low-latency routes, and to enable experimental deep-loop-pruning heuristics.

Trade-offs: + Provides safer, auditable result injection and prevents silent loop amplification. - Adds memory/CPU overhead per request and small commit latency; mitigations include tunable caps and fast-path bypass for trusted internal routes.
acceptance_criteria: Staging buffer implemented with enforced per-request memory cap and GC on request end
Injection commit validates schema and applies atomic deltas to streaming output
Recursion guard detects repeated (tool_id, input_hash) pairs and blocks further invocations with structured error code 'TOOL_LOOP_DETECTED'
Compatibility adapter returns commit_id when commit can't complete within the legacy wait window and the follow-up polling URL resolves to the final committed output
End-to-end integration tests covering streaming + tool calls + nested tool invocations up to depth 8 with expected guard behavior
Metrics for loop detection and commit latency are available on the runtime dashboard and alert at threshold

risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Increased per-request memory leading to OOM on noisy tenants. Mitigation: enforce strict caps, per-tenant admission control, and fast-path bypass flag for trusted routes.

Risk: False-positive loop detections because of non-deterministic tool outputs. Mitigation: use normalized input hashing and configurable fuzz-tolerance window; provide operator override to replay suspicious requests.
Risk: Legacy SDKs break if compatibility adapter misbehaves. Mitigation: staged rollout with feature flag and telemetry to detect adapter timeouts and client errors.
Risk: Sensitive data in staging logs. Mitigation: HMAC tamper-evidence, 30s ephemeral retention, and automatic redaction based on disclosure policy.
open_questions: What should the default invocation depth be for customer-facing routes vs internal-only routes?
Should the Bloom filter be per-request only or shared across a short window to detect cross-request loops?
Is the 800ms legacy wait window sufficient for common tool runtimes (DB lookups, external APIs)?
Do we need a visible UI in Console to inspect staging snapshots when a loop is detected?
